precepts.why:
“I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid.” The answer is no: God has not cast away the 12 tribes of Israel. “For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.” Read that first verse on the street and it tells you what the subject is about.

Paul speaks of “a remnant according to the election of grace.” Who is the elect? Isaiah says: “For Jacob my servant’s sake, and Israel mine elect, I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me.” We are the elect. Israel is the elect, not all nations. This is where Paul is getting that from.

Paul even says “God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew”: there is that word again, the same as Romans 8:29, so we did not even have to go to Amos 3; Paul deals with it here. Elijah thought he was by himself, but God answered, “I have reserved to myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to the image of Baal.” The elect remnant is Israel.

“And so all Israel shall be saved”. And so, meaning as a result of all that has been said: all 12 tribes shall be saved. “For this is my covenant unto them”: unto the 12 tribes of Israel, the elect of Isaiah 45.

Nehemiah shows what the works are: “For the shewbread, and for the continual meat offering, and for the continual burnt offering, of the sabbaths, of the new moons, for the set feasts, and for the holy things, and for the sin offerings to make an atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.”

Stress that last part: “all the work of the house of our God.” Those are the works Paul is speaking of: the works of the temple, the works of animal sacrifice, the offerings and things of that nature.

So the remnant chosen by grace is not chosen by the temple works of sacrifice and offering; it does not throw away the commandments. The elect of Israel are kept by grace, and all Israel shall be saved.

note.label: Raising Up the Tabernacle of David That Fell

precepts.why:
“And if some of the branches be broken off”. The branches broken off are Judah. Jeremiah shows the olive tree and its breaking: “The Lord called thy name, A green olive tree, fair, and of goodly fruit: with the noise of a great tumult he hath kindled fire upon it, and the branches of it are broken.”

God himself named his people a green olive tree, fair and of goodly fruit. That is the tree Paul speaks of. And the fire kindled on it with a great tumult is how the branches came to be broken.

Why were they broken? Paul answers: “because of unbelief they were broken off”. Judah's unbelief caused them to be broken off.

So when the wild olive tree, the northern kingdom, is graffed in among them, it is graffed into God's own green olive tree. “Boast not against the branches”: do not boast against Judah. “thou bearest not the root, but the root thee”. The root is Christ, and Christ is the one that keeps the northern kingdom graffed in with Judah. “Be not highminded, but fear: For if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee.”

precepts.why:
“and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them”. That is what Ezekiel 37 shows: “Moreover, thou son of man, take thee one stick, and write upon it, For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions: then take another stick, and write upon it, For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel his companions”.

“And join them one to another into one stick; and they shall become one in thine hand.” That is the grafting: the stick of Joseph, Ephraim and the house of Israel, joined to the stick of Judah, and the two become one in God's hand.

So the wild olive tree is not the nations; it is the northern kingdom being joined back with Judah. That is why Paul warns, “Boast not against the branches.” Zechariah 12:7 says the same: that they do not magnify themselves against Judah. That magnify is telling you: do not be highminded, do not boast.

“Be not highminded, but fear”. The root that bears the graffed-in branch is Christ, and he is the one that holds the two sticks together as one.

note.label: The Pride Of Thine Heart Hath Deceived Thee!

precepts.why:
Some Israelite camps use “all Israel shall be saved” to argue that even the wicked will escape hell. To see what Paul meant, start from the beginning of the chapter: “I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.”

Why did Paul open that way? Because of the conflict between the northern and southern kingdoms. The Jews thought God was not dealing with the northern kingdom anymore, since God had told them, you are not my people, and Hosea said that where it was said unto them, you are not my people, there they would be called the children of the living God. Paul, of Benjamin, was of the southern kingdom, and he answers, “God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew.”

“For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.” The mystery is that God is dealing with both the northern and southern kingdoms, which is why the chapter talks about them being grafted back in. God blinded a portion, the Jews, to salvation in Jesus Christ so that the gospel could be preached to the northern kingdom living as Gentiles, so they could come in. If you say you're an Israelite and you still don't understand this chapter after all these years, you're an idiot, and God is not dealing with you.

“And so all Israel shall be saved”. That means both kingdoms, all twelve tribes, can be saved. It is not a license saying a murderer, an adulterer or a thief will be saved at the end no matter what. You see how stupid they are? Leaders who use this verse to say you are not going to hell are wise in their own conceits. There is a hell, and if you go against God you are going into it, Israelite or not.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walk Through of Romans 5

precepts.why:
If sin reigned unto death over the chosen line, has God given up on them? Paul answers: “I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.”

“God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew.” Which he foreknew: that is Amos 3 and Romans 8 again. “You only have I known of all the families of the earth”, and “whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate”.

The cycle Ezra described, the righteous line receiving the law, going off, being destroyed and repenting, never ended with God throwing his people away. Every time, out of that line the righteous rose up again.

So where sin abounded, grace did much more abound, and it abounded upon the same people God foreknew. Paul, an Israelite of Benjamin, is himself the proof that God has not cast away his people.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
Romans 11:5 speaks of “a remnant according to the election of grace”, and verse 6 goes on: “And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace.” If by grace, meaning Christ's death, his mercy: Christ's death granted us grace, his sacrifice granted us grace. So what are the works? Nehemiah shows them.

“For the shewbread, and for the continual meat offering, and for the continual burnt offering, of the sabbaths, of the new moons, for the set feasts, and for the holy things, and for the sin offerings to make an atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.” The works are the sacrifices and temple ordinances, which were still around when Paul wrote the letter, because the temple had not yet been destroyed. Israel was still doing them.

So “no more of works” means no more sacrifice. We are not being called based upon animals we sacrifice; we are being called based upon our acceptance of Christ's death on the cross and of him being the Messiah. It is no more of works once Christ died.

“otherwise grace is no more grace”: if we are still regarding and accepting the sacrificing of animals, then Christ's death is void. Then we put Christ to the back and just keep sacrificing animals. “But if it be of works, then is it no more grace”: then you put Christ out of the way, no more Messiah. “otherwise work is no more work”: the sacrifice is done away with, because Christ died on the cross.

precepts.why:
Romans 11:12 says “Now if the fall of them be the riches of the world, and the diminishing of them the riches of the Gentiles”. The fall of them is the builders, the leaders of the southern kingdom, rejecting Christ, and the diminishing is the same thing in different wording: something that decays, drops lower, falls. What are the riches of the world? Is it talking about money? No: the kingdom. The Pharisees had to reject Christ because it was their lot; Christ had to be killed, and once he died on that cross he granted us access to the kingdom. That is the riches of the world.

And who is the world? Some say, world is Israel, where did you get that from? World is world. No, it's not. The world is us: “But Israel shall be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation: ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end.” Israel is the world without end.

Christ says the same in Mark 10:30: “in the world to come eternal life.” The world to come is our kingdom, eternal life. That is the riches of the world.

So when Romans 11:15 says “if the casting away of them be the reconciling of the world”, it is speaking of Israel. To reconcile is to bring back together what was together before, and the nations were never together with us.

Romans 11:11 says the leaders' fall brought salvation to the Gentiles “for to provoke them to jealousy”, as Moses said: “I will provoke you to jealousy by them that are no people”. The ones provoked are the southern kingdom, and the ones who are no people are the northern kingdom, who received Christ. But the southern kingdom still comes first.

“The Lord also shall save the tents of Judah first, that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem do not magnify themselves against Judah.” He will raise the tents of Judah first.

Paul says it too: the gospel of Christ “is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.” The Jew is Judah, first; the Greek is the northern kingdom. And judgment runs in the same order: “Tribulation and anguish, upon every soul of man that doeth evil, of the Jew first, and also of the Gentile”.

That is why Romans 11 says God has not cast away his people. Judah stumbled, but Judah is saved first, and the northern kingdom that received Christ provokes them to jealousy until they come in.

precepts.why:
Here is Romans 11:11 happening in history. “But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with envy”: that is Judah, filled with jealousy. They “spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming.”

“Then Paul and Barnabas waxed bold, and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you”: to the southern kingdom, first. “but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.” They rejected it, so Paul turned to the Gentiles, who are not a people: the northern kingdom.

You won't find it in the Bible that Israel rejected the prophets and the prophets went to the Arabs. Isaiah never said, they reject me, I'm going to go talk to the Philistines. Lo, we turn to the East Indians, lo, we turn to the Chinese? Christ is black and you're not, there are twelve gates and your name's not on them, but serve him anyway? That makes no sense. Whether you are a black Hebrew Israelite or a Christian, if you teach that, you hate your people. He showeth his word unto Jacob and has not dealt so with any other nation, and still you look for some way to save the people who destroyed, raped, robbed and murdered your people, and don't want judgment to come to them.

So the Gentiles Paul turned to were his own flesh, the northern kingdom, “for to provoke them to jealousy”, that he might “provoke to emulation them which are my flesh, and might save some of them.”

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
“For if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy”. Who is the firstfruit? Paul answers it in Corinthians: “But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming.”

Christ is the firstfruits. It starts with Christ, because he is our creator, the rock that begat us, and then it goes to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as well. “Afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming” means the elect.

And the lump is Israel. If the firstfruit is holy, the lump is also holy: because Christ is holy, the people that come after him in his order are holy too.

So Romans 11 opens by tying Israel to Christ. The same holy firstfruit stands at the head of the whole lump, and that is why God has not cast away his people. Both kingdoms, the branches that fell and the branches grafted back in, belong to that holy lump that follows Christ.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.why:
“And if the root be holy, so are the branches.” Who is the root? Christ says it himself: “I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David”.

And who are the branches? Christ said in John 15, “I am the vine, ye are the branches.” The branches go into the offspring, the children: us. If the root is holy, so are the branches that grow out of him.

That is what “the root and fatness of the olive tree” is in verse 17. Both kingdoms partake of Christ; he rules over them both. And it is why Paul warns, “Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee.” If you boast against your brothers, you are not following Christ; it is Christ, the root, that bears you.

So the root being holy is the reason the natural branches can be grafted in again and the wild branches can be grafted in at all. Everything grows out of Christ, the root and offspring of David.

Hosea shows why Ephraim is called wild: “For they are gone up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by himself: Ephraim hath hired lovers.” Ephraim is a wild ass alone by himself; a wild ass or a wild olive tree, it is the northern kingdom gone off into idolatry.

That is why Paul, speaking as the apostle of the Gentiles, writes to the southern kingdom while also addressing the northern kingdom: you that I am writing to were also a wild olive tree. And that is why the grafting is “contrary to nature”: the northern kingdom was uncircumcised, in uncleanness, scattered abroad afar off, not a people, and hated by the southern kingdom.

Grafting in goes into reconciling: bringing the two back together again. You can only graft an olive tree into an olive tree; you cannot graft a mango tree into an olive tree. The wild branches are the same kind as the natural ones: Israel.

Then watch who that olive tree is: “For the Lord of hosts, that planted thee, hath pronounced evil against thee, for the evil of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah, which they have done against themselves to provoke me to anger in offering incense unto Baal.” The house of Israel first, the house of Judah second: both houses.

So the olive tree refers to both the house of Israel and the house of Judah. The wild olive tree is not the other nations; the nations are never called olive trees.

That is how Romans 11 ends: “God is able to graff them in again.” Again, because they were always there. “And so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob: For this is my covenant unto them, when I shall take away their sins.” Their sins, Jacob’s sins, all twelve tribes. The white man did many sins on this earth, and the Lord is not taking his sins away; he is going to pay for them. “God hath concluded them all in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all”: all Israel.

A graft is a shoot or twig inserted into a slit on the trunk or stem of a living plant, from which it receives sap. You take one piece of plant and put it to another, and you graft them together, so that that twig lives and flourishes based on the one that’s rooted and grounded.

“For God is able to graff them in again”: meaning bring them back again. Notice the word again, because Christians on the street will try to pull this on you, that it’s talking about white people and other nations. Oh no. When was Esau grafted in? When were the Philistines with us, or the Moabites? Never. It’s talking about Israel.

“For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature”: this is the northern kingdom. We were wild by nature, disobedient. “And wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree”: the Lord brought you, northern kingdom, back. “How much more shall these, which be the natural branches”: the kingdom of Judah, “be graffed into their own olive tree?”

points: “For this is my covenant unto them”: them who? Them Israelites. “When I shall take away their sins.” This whole thing is about Israel (Hebrews 8:8).
